item.title: Strategy Under Extreme Institutional Shock: Scenario Planning, Foresight, and Strategic Management in the Face of Radical Uncertainty
item.content:encoded:
James Bezjian, The Citadel Military College of South Carolina

Jose Godinez, University of Massachusetts Lowell

Veselina Stoyanova, University of Birmingham

Arpit Sharma, The Citadel Military College of South Carolina

This special issue in the Journal of Strategy and Management examines how organizations respond strategically when major disruptions fundamentally alter the institutional environment and challenge established decision-making frameworks. The focus is on situations where core assumptions, sources of authority, and environmental interpretation become uncertain or contested, requiring organizations to develop new approaches to strategic adaptation and resilience.

The special issue addresses contemporary challenges highlighted by recent global crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical instability, climate disasters, cyber threats, and artificial intelligence advances. By studying how organizations interpret uncertainty, maintain legitimacy, and navigate institutional disruption, the work contributes insights valuable to business leaders, policymakers, and public sector organizations seeking to strengthen resilience amid increasing volatility.

Appel publié par Journal of strategy and management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Extreme institutional shocks and strategy theory
  • High-impact, low-probability events and strategic decision-making
  • Dynamic capabilities under radical novelty and epistemic uncertainty
  • Organizational resilience and adaptation under Knightian uncertainty
  • Strategic responses to pandemics, climate tipping points, and AI discontinuities
  • Institutional legitimacy and re-legitimation following paradigm shocks
  • Managerial sensemaking and cognitive framing under extreme ambiguity
  • Strategy-as-practice during institutional disruption
  • Real options reasoning under Knightian uncertainty
  • Strategic foresight and scenario planning for paradigm-breaking events

Timeline

  • March 30, 2027: Full paper submission deadline
  • January 1, 2029: Publication date of special issue

item.title: Strategy and Aesthetics
item.content:encoded:
René Wiedner, Warwick Business School

Jennifer Whyte, University of Sydney

Saku Mantere, McGill University

Robin Holt, University of Bristol

Marie-Léandre Gomez, ESSEC Business School

There is broad recognition that organizational life cannot be fully understood or managed through rationalist frameworks. Scholars across the social sciences, including human geography and cultural theory, have long acknowledged how sensory experience, emotion, affect and embodied practice shape organization. Strategy studies are also beginning to understand how strategically significant phenomena–organizational routines, capabilities and identity, investment allocation and judgment, leadership, environmental adaptation–refuse to be confined to, and by, rational, logically structured analyses.

There is an aesthetic aspect to all strategy–it is as much vision as it reason; as much inspiration as analysis. Emotions, feelings, intuitions, desires and instincts can all have strategically significant influence. The symbolic and material dimensions of organising, alongside questions of purpose and structure across multiple human practices and fields, are all factors for which a successful strategic design must take account. The discursive, ecological and commercial forces to which organizations are adapting continually are encountered in aesthetic terms.

Appel publié par Strategic Organization. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The aesthetic qualities of strategy work: combining creative expression with analytical rigor; the coexistence of, and interplay between, poetics and reason
  • Aesthetically-infused experiences such as awe in understanding how strategic organizations resist the disenchantment of strategy work through over-rationalization
  • Studies of strategy confronting cultural landscapes encouraging the production and consumption of styles rather than goods, posing complex strategic identity choices across audiences with different stylistic preferences and evaluation criteria
  • How the strategic organization of affective forces is often caught in a fundamental ambiguity between instrumental organization and unmanageable reorganization of experience
  • Examinations of analogue and digital strategic devices and how these contribute to the performance of strategic styles, including strategy work in boardrooms and informal organizing contexts
  • Investigations of the strategic appropriation of artistic activity and how organizations draw from artistic practices to reinvent themselves and maximize profitability
  • Studies of organizational design and the formation of capabilities and identities that can be structured to elicit strategically significant commitments amongst stakeholders
  • Inquiries of processual forming and formation in strategy, invoking vitalist and new materialist philosophy and questions about organizational forms
  • Engagements with the raw material of strategy in formation, including how information and data have aesthetic forms and dimensions
  • Connecting strategy and temporality through aesthetics, including how strategy forms narrative plots that elicit specific feelings of progression, symbolic and communal attachments, and identities

item.title: Unpacking Digitalization: Antecedents, Strategies, and Performance Implications
item.content:encoded:
Jasmina Berbegal-Mirabent, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya

Angelo Cavallo, Politecnico di Milano

Antje Fiedler, University of Auckland

Esteban Lafuente, Instituto Tecnológico de Costa Rica

Digital transformation has become essential for both private and public organizations seeking innovation and competitive advantage. However, the literature lacks coherent understanding of how digitalization is implemented across different contexts. While large organizations traditionally led these efforts, SMEs and public institutions increasingly must engage in digital transformation despite significant resource constraints.

The relationship between digitalization and performance is complex and context-dependent. Digital technologies offer opportunities for innovation and efficiency but also carry risks of misalignment with strategy and organizational disruption. Success requires aligning digital initiatives with organizational capabilities, workforce skills, and strategic planning rather than technology adoption alone.

This special issue seeks contributions examining how organizations manage digitalization efforts across private firms and public institutions, addressing the drivers of digital transformation, mechanisms through which digitalization influences performance outcomes, and how digital transformation reshapes competitive dynamics in different economic contexts.
